title: The Superiority of Prophecy over Tongues
english: When someone speaks in a tongue, what profit is there in the words, since no one understands them except God, who knows all things?
The apostle says that one speaks mysteries by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 14:2).
But observe how the one speaking to God speaks by the Spirit; therefore, the Spirit is God.
So then, the one speaking in a tongue speaks more to God and not to men, as the apostle says.
On the other hand, the one prophesying speaks to men for edification, exhortation, and consolation.

Understanding that prophecy consists in these things, it follows that to interpret is the work of the prophets; through which the word of the one being encouraged is confirmed, and the mind of the initiated is led by the hand into the truth that is upon Christ.

This also pre-demonstrates, in a way that is better than speaking in a tongue, the task of interpreting the things of the prophets, and indeed, it is better in the superior things of speaking in a tongue.
For the one speaking in a tongue edifies himself, as the apostle says (1 Corinthians 14:4), for he himself understands, but for another, it is wholly nothing.
But the one who uses the voices and prophecies of the holy prophets for testimony edifies the church.
Therefore, prophecy is greater, both in the highest matters and in bright hopes; if indeed it is admittedly better to edify the church, than to converse with himself alone in a tongue.
The apostle says, 'I want all of you to speak in tongues, but rather that you may prophesy' (1 Corinthians 14:5).

Since it was paradoxical and truly God-given for men, who were Hebrews, to be able to speak in other tongues, as seen in Acts 2:4, no one might think the apostle is determining that which is fitting to say having been given through the energy of the Spirit; for it is given as a sign to the faithful.

He accepts the matter and says, 'I want all of you to speak in tongues.', then immediately and clearly cuts off the zeal for this matter, shifting instead toward what is better by moving straightly toward it.
Rather, he moves so that you may prophesy, making the one who prophesies with tongues even greater by speaking with utmost clarity.

He demonstrates that this is not entirely unlearned to those who possess the gift and to those who are listening; for it brings forth nothing unless it is being interpreted—that is, unless there is someone always sitting by to interpret for those being initiated.
And nothing of their actions is intelligible.
Let some enter into the churches having been enriched by the energy of the Spirit with the ability to speak in tongues.
It is then necessary that they offer prayers in them, and before these, supplications or psalmody.

Otherwise, if they are merely able to use the tongue of those present, this is not a matter of spiritual thrones; instead, being swelled up by the gift of tongues alone, they perform neither prayers nor psalmody.

Paul teaches this: if the hearers are not experts in the tongue with which the one possessing the gift is conversing, there is no profit from the practice, for there are myriads of nations and many tongues among men.
Nothing of those who perform once in rational matters, or among men, is intelligible.
He says 'unintelligible' entirely regarding nothing of those performing in rational matters—that is, among men.

For unless someone happens to know the meaning, the power of each individual voice is lost; even if those listening were experts in his own tongue, they would be barbarians to one another, even though they are speaking correctly according to each person's own voice.
It is therefore necessary to teach others who are willing, so that the habit of searching out the word for the listeners may be maintained.
But if the sound was insignificant and the voice was unusual, he has acted in vain, striking only the hearing of the learner with some random blow.
He says that those who wish to teach must speak a word that is common to the hearers, since otherwise he labors in vain.
For it is not by speaking in single languages that the church is built up.
As the apostle says, 'If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays' (1 Corinthians 14:14).
The Spirit is at work in these things through the power of prayer and prophecy.

title: Tongues and Understanding
english: The gift of the Spirit is the ability to speak in tongues, which is the power to speak in languages.
If I pray in the Spirit, using the language given through the Spirit, my mind will be unfruitful.
In prayers, one must strive together and seek the things that lead to salvation from God, not to be puffed up by language and simply to speak in tongues.
For if I were to speak empty sounds, I would be like a sounding brass (1 Corinthians 13:1).
For if I were to speak in tongues without understanding, my mind would be unfruitful, and I would not receive any benefit from such ambition.
I will pray in the Spirit, and I will also pray with my mind.
If I wish to pray in tongues, I must strive earnestly not to have an unfruitful mind, nor to be alone in speaking in tongues, but to arouse my mind.
And if I were to sing in tongues, I would not neglect to understand the power of the psalm and the prophecy with my mind.
For it is better to prophesy or interpret the divine scriptures in the church than to simply speak in tongues.
What then is the better thing? I will pray in the Spirit, and I will pray also with my mind.
When we bless with the spirit, the person who is taking the place of the layperson cannot say 'Amen' because they do not understand what is being said.
This is a problem because, in the churches, it is customary for the people to follow the prayers of their leaders with their own assent, bringing to completion the voice of the priest.
By doing so, what seems to be lacking in the perfection of the priests is filled by the measures of the people, and God receives both the small and the great in unity of spirit.
The people under their care join their own prayers to those of the priests, believing that they will be accepted by God.
This is why God has also commanded that even poor sacrifices be brought to the altar, so that the small, mixed with the perfect, may become acceptable to God.
For we are all one in the Lord.
And when we speak in a tongue, we are blessing with the spirit.
However, if the person listening does not know what we are saying, they cannot say 'Amen' to their own prayer, and therefore they are not edified.
It is essential that all things be done for our edification and for the benefit of our brothers.
The proclamation of all good things is truly for those who have received faith.
In this proclamation, it is said that they stand firm and are saved.
The fact that they stand indicates that they have stability in their hope and are in a state of good glory, having believed.
And the fact that they are saved means that this salvation has also been revealed to them.

title: Resurrection
english: Christ's death and resurrection are the foundation of our faith, and it is through these events that we are freed from the bonds of sin and death, running beyond the bonds of death to attain a state better than sin.

The gospel, which was delivered to us by the apostles, is the message of salvation that has been revealed to us through the revelation of Jesus Christ, and it is not something that came into mind simply and without torture, but rather it is the gospel that the apostle received, with the knowledge of the one who became human for us, as he himself said, 'Not even I received it from man, nor was I taught, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ' (Galatians 1:12).

If the one delivering the gospel is taught by God, how can it not be true what is preached through him, that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, clearly of both the old and new testaments?
Many have borne witness to Christ's death and resurrection.

Through his death and resurrection, Christ has removed the sin of the world and given us the gift of eternal life, and it is necessary to say not only that he died, but also that he was buried, for the Emmanuel, being truly dead, is placed in a tomb.

But he lived again, as I said a little while ago, and through his death in the flesh, he confirms that he became flesh, although he is God, the Word, and through his trampling of death, he clearly shows that he is God by nature, and the Word from God the Father is not foreign to giving life to the temple, but rather it is his own body, through which he is said to have died for us, so that the good of resurrection might truly be found for us.

For the whole human nature was in him trampling death; thus we are said to be buried and risen with him, to sit and be in heavenly places, and he is said to have risen according to the scriptures, to have appeared to the holy apostles, and to some in part and in multitude, and he appeared to me also as to one of the lowliest of the apostles.

The church is being persecuted and strengthened, except that we have been pitied and called by Christ to apostleship, and the great mystery of the resurrection is not unknown to the ancient saints, for it has been revealed to them, and if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how can some among you claim that there is no resurrection of the dead?

It is astonishing that some are persuaded otherwise, contrary to the sacred and divine scriptures, and dare to think differently, for if Christ died not to remain dead, but to be found stronger than death and corruption, and to become a way and door for human nature to be able to overcome corruption and return to life, then it is puzzling that the bonds of death still hold sway over those for whom God is said to have died and been raised according to his nature, being Emmanuel.

What is being denied to human nature, the benefits that come from resurrection, and why is the culmination of the flesh's economy being slandered, for if Christ has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep and the firstborn from the dead, then it is only logical that the rest will follow the firstfruits, and will be in company with the firstborn, as is fitting for the firstborn, and the apostle Paul himself testifies to this, saying...
When Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, it is equivalent to saying that he has been raised from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:12).
